Probabilistic graphical models

A graph drawn over random variables turns an exponentially large joint distribution into a product of small local factors — and the same graph tells you which inferences are easy, which are hard, and how to approximate the rest.

blocks.html:
1. Bayesian networks

A joint distribution over $n$ binary variables has $2^n-1$ free parameters — hopeless to store or learn for any interesting $n$. A Bayesian network tames this by drawing a directed acyclic graph (DAG) over the variables and asserting that each variable depends directly only on its parents. The chain rule for a DAG then factorizes the joint into a product of small local conditionals:

$p(x_1,\dots,x_n)=\prod_{i=1}^{n} p\big(x_i \mid \mathrm{pa}(i)\big),$

where $\mathrm{pa}(i)$ is the set of parents of node $i$. Each factor is a small conditional probability table indexed only by a node and its parents, so the parameter count drops from exponential in $n$ to a sum of small local tables.

Worked mini-example — counting parameters. Take the classic alarm network with $C\to A$, $C\to R$ (a cause $C$ with two effects $A,R$), all binary. The factorization $p(C)\,p(A \mid C)\,p(R \mid C)$ needs $1+2+2=5$ parameters. The full joint over three binary variables needs $2^3-1=7$. The savings grow explosively with the network: structure is compression.

Conditional independence and d-separation

The graph encodes more than a factorization — it encodes a whole list of conditional independence statements, read off purely topologically by d-separation. A path between $A$ and $B$ is blocked by a conditioning set $Z$ according to the three local structures it passes through:

  • Chain $A\to C\to B$: blocked iff $C\in Z$.
  • Fork $A\leftarrow C\to B$ (common cause): blocked iff $C\in Z$.
  • Collider $A\to C\leftarrow B$ (common effect, the v-structure): blocked iff neither $C$ nor any descendant of $C$ is in $Z$.

If every path from $A$ to $B$ is blocked by $Z$, then $A\perp B \mid Z$. The collider rule is the famous trap and runs opposite to the other two: an unobserved collider blocks the path (so $A\perp B$ marginally), while observing the collider — or any of its descendants — opens it, making $A$ and $B$ dependent. This is explaining away: two independent causes of an observed effect become coupled once the effect is known.

Worked mini-example — a collider query. In the network $\text{Rain}\to\text{WetGrass}\leftarrow\text{Sprinkler}$, rain and the sprinkler are independent causes: $\text{Rain}\perp\text{Sprinkler}$. But once you observe wet grass, learning it did not rain makes the sprinkler more likely — they are now dependent: $\text{Rain}\not\perp\text{Sprinkler}\mid\text{WetGrass}$. Observing the collider opened the path.

Toggle evidence on the sprinkler/rain/wet-grass network below, read off the factorization and a posterior, and run a d-separation query to watch the collider rule flip the verdict.

2. Markov random fields

Not every dependency has a natural direction. Pixels in an image, spins in a magnet, words in a sentence influence their neighbors symmetrically. For these we use an undirected graphical model — a Markov random field (MRF), also called a Markov network. There are no parents and no conditional tables; instead the joint factorizes over the cliques of the graph as a product of nonnegative potentials $\psi_c$:

$p(x)=\frac1Z\prod_{c\in\mathcal{C}}\psi_c(x_c),\qquad Z=\sum_{x}\prod_{c}\psi_c(x_c).$

Writing each potential as $\psi_c(x_c)=\exp(-E_c(x_c))$ turns the product into the Gibbs / Boltzmann form

$p(x)=\frac1Z\exp\!\Big(-\sum_{c} E_c(x_c)\Big),$

where $E_c$ is the energy of clique $c$ and $Z$ is the partition function. Low-energy configurations are exponentially more probable; the temperature (built into the scale of $E$) controls how sharply.

Hammersley–Clifford. The deep fact tying the graph to the factorization: for a strictly positive distribution $p(x) > 0$, $p$ is Markov with respect to a graph $G$ (i.e. separation in $G$ implies conditional independence) if and only if $p$ is a Gibbs distribution factoring over the cliques of $G$. Strict positivity cannot be dropped — deterministic constraints (zeros in $p$) can satisfy the Markov property without admitting a clique factorization.

The Markov blanket

In an MRF the Markov blanket of a node is simply its set of graph neighbors: conditioned on its neighbors, a node is independent of every other variable. Hence the full conditional simplifies dramatically,

$p(x_i \mid x_{-i}) = p\big(x_i \mid x_{\mathcal{N}(i)}\big)\propto \prod_{c\ni i}\psi_c(x_c),$

and — crucially — the intractable global $Z$ cancels, leaving only a local normalization over the few values of $x_i$. This is exactly what makes Gibbs sampling (§6) cheap. (In a directed network the blanket is larger: parents, children, and the children's other co-parents.)

Worked mini-example — the Ising model. Spins $x_i\in\{-1,+1\}$ on a grid with edge potentials favoring agreement: $E=-J\sum_{(i,j)\in\text{edges}} x_i x_j$. The full conditional of one spin is $p(x_i=+1 \mid x_{\mathcal{N}(i)})=\sigma\!\big(2J\sum_{j\in\mathcal{N}(i)} x_j\big)$, a logistic in the sum of its four neighbors — local, and $Z$-free. At low temperature (large $J$) neighbors align into large domains; at high temperature the grid is a random speckle.

Slide the temperature on a small Ising grid below and watch the energy, the magnetization, and the local conditional of the highlighted spin respond.

params.hint: lower temperature ⇒ neighbors align; the conditional uses only the Markov blanket. The button runs stochastic Gibbs sweeps (sampling), not deterministic energy minimization.
params.svgTitle: A 6 by 6 Ising grid colored by spin, with the energy and a single spin's full conditional from its four neighbors

3. Exact inference

Having a compact factorization is only half the battle; we still need to answer queries. The two basic ones are the marginal $p(x_q)=\sum_{x_{-q}}p(x)$ — summing out everything but the query — and the MAP $\arg\max_x p(x)$. Done naively, the sum runs over exponentially many configurations. Variable elimination makes it tractable by exploiting distributivity: a sum only interacts with the factors that mention the variable being summed.

$\sum_{x_k}\prod_{c}\psi_c(x_c) = \Big(\prod_{c:\,x_k\notin c}\psi_c\Big)\underbrace{\sum_{x_k}\prod_{c:\,x_k\in c}\psi_c}_{\text{new factor }\tau(\cdot)}.$

So to eliminate $x_k$: gather the factors containing it, multiply them, sum out $x_k$, and reinsert the resulting factor $\tau$ over the remaining variables. Repeat down an elimination order until only the query remains.

Worked mini-example — a chain marginal. For the chain MRF $X_1 - X_2 - X_3 - X_4$ with pairwise potentials, compute $p(x_4)$ by eliminating left to right: $\tau_2(x_2)=\sum_{x_1}\psi_{12}(x_1,x_2)$, then $\tau_3(x_3)=\sum_{x_2}\psi_{23}(x_2,x_3)\,\tau_2(x_2)$, then $\tau_4(x_4)=\sum_{x_3}\psi_{34}(x_3,x_4)\,\tau_3(x_3)$, and normalize. Every intermediate factor is over a single variable, so each step is cheap — the chain has treewidth 1.

Treewidth — the cost of inference

The expense is not the number of variables but the size of the largest intermediate factor produced. When you eliminate a variable you create a factor over all of its current neighbors, which also adds fill-in edges connecting those neighbors. The largest such scope, over the best possible elimination order, defines the treewidth of the graph, and the running time is exponential in it:

$\text{cost}\approx \sum_k (\text{values})^{\,|\text{factor at step }k|}\ =\ O\!\big(n\cdot v^{\,w+1}\big),$

with $w$ the induced width of the order and $v$ the variable arity. Trees and chains have $w=1$ (linear-time inference); a dense $m\times m$ grid has $w=O(m)$ (intractable). Choosing the optimal order is itself NP-hard, but good heuristics (min-fill, min-degree) work well. The junction tree algorithm organizes the surviving factors into a tree of cliques so that all marginals can be read off in one calibration — the foundation of belief propagation in §4.

Pick an elimination order on a small chain network below and watch the factors combine step by step into the requested marginal — and see the induced width the order produces.

params.hint: step through the eliminations; watch factors combine into the marginal

4. Belief propagation

Variable elimination answers one marginal at a time and repeats work for each query. Belief propagation (BP), the sum–product algorithm, computes all marginals at once by passing local messages along the edges of a factor graph — a bipartite graph with a node for each variable and a square node for each factor. Two kinds of message flow:

$\mu_{x\to f}(x)=\!\!\prod_{g\in\mathcal{N}(x)\setminus f}\!\!\mu_{g\to x}(x),\qquad \mu_{f\to x}(x)=\sum_{x_{\mathcal{N}(f)\setminus x}}\!\! f(x_{\mathcal{N}(f)})\!\!\prod_{y\in\mathcal{N}(f)\setminus x}\!\!\mu_{y\to f}(y).$

A variable's message to a factor is the product of everything it has heard from its other factors; a factor's message to a variable sums the factor against everything it has heard from its other variables. Once messages have flowed, the marginal at a node is the (normalized) product of all incoming factor messages:

$p(x)\ \propto\ \prod_{f\in\mathcal{N}(x)}\mu_{f\to x}(x).$

Exact on trees. When the factor graph is a tree, there is a unique path between any two nodes, so messages never double-count. A single sweep of leaves-to-root followed by root-to-leaves messages computes every marginal exactly — belief propagation is variable elimination run simultaneously in all directions, sharing the intermediate factors. This is the junction-tree calibration of §3 specialized to a tree.

Loopy belief propagation

On a graph with cycles the message equations still make sense, and iterating them — loopy BP — is one of the most successful approximate inference methods (it underlies modern error-correcting decoders). But the guarantees evaporate: evidence can circulate around a loop and be counted more than once, the iteration may oscillate rather than converge, and even at a fixed point the marginals are only approximate. It works astonishingly well in practice on many graphs nonetheless.

Worked mini-example — a three-node chain. For the tree factor graph $X_1 - f_{12} - X_2 - f_{23} - X_3$, the message from the left leaf is $\mu_{f_{12}\to X_2}(x_2)=\sum_{x_1} f_{12}(x_1,x_2)\,\mu_{X_1\to f_{12}}(x_1)$, and symmetrically from the right. The marginal $p(x_2)\propto\mu_{f_{12}\to X_2}(x_2)\,\mu_{f_{23}\to X_2}(x_2)$ — the two halves of the chain meet at $X_2$. Compare with the §3 elimination: same arithmetic, organized for reuse.

Step the messages through a small tree factor graph below and watch them combine into the node marginals — exactly, in two sweeps.

blocks.html:
5. Variational inference

When the graph has high treewidth and loopy BP is unreliable, we abandon exactness and optimize instead. Variational inference picks a tractable family $\mathcal{Q}$ and finds the member $q(z)$ closest to the true posterior $p(z \mid x)$ in Kullback–Leibler divergence:

$q^\star=\arg\min_{q\in\mathcal{Q}}\ \mathrm{KL}\big(q(z)\,\|\,p(z \mid x)\big).$

We cannot evaluate that KL directly — it contains the intractable $p(z \mid x)$. The trick is the evidence lower bound (ELBO). Starting from $\log p(x)$ and inserting $q$,

$\log p(x) = \underbrace{\mathbb{E}_{q}\!\big[\log p(x,z)\big]-\mathbb{E}_{q}\!\big[\log q(z)\big]}_{\mathrm{ELBO}(q)}\ +\ \underbrace{\mathrm{KL}\big(q(z)\,\|\,p(z \mid x)\big)}_{\ge\, 0}.$

The key inequality. Since $\mathrm{KL}\ge 0$ always (with equality iff $q=p(\cdot \mid x)$), the identity gives $\mathrm{ELBO}(q)=\log p(x)-\mathrm{KL}\le\log p(x)$ — the ELBO is a lower bound on the log-evidence. And because $\log p(x)$ does not depend on $q$, maximizing the ELBO is exactly minimizing $\mathrm{KL}(q\,\|\,p(\cdot \mid x))$. The intractable posterior never appears in the ELBO — only the tractable joint $p(x,z)$ and the entropy of $q$ — so we can actually optimize it.

Mean-field and coordinate ascent

The simplest tractable family is mean-field: assume $q$ factorizes over the latent variables,

$q(z)=\prod_{j} q_j(z_j).$

Holding every other factor fixed and maximizing the ELBO over $q_j$ gives the closed-form coordinate-ascent (CAVI) update

$\log q_j(z_j)\ =\ \mathbb{E}_{q_{-j}}\!\big[\log p(x,z)\big] + \text{const},$

i.e. each factor is the expected log-joint under the other factors, exponentiated and normalized. Cycling these updates monotonically increases the ELBO to a local optimum. The price of the factorization: $q$ cannot represent posterior correlations, and mean-field characteristically underestimates posterior variance.

Worked mini-example — the ELBO gap. Approximate a correlated bivariate Gaussian posterior by a factorized $q=q_1(z_1)q_2(z_2)$. CAVI drives $q$ to the product of the conditionals' shapes; as it iterates, the ELBO climbs toward $\log p(x)$ and the gap $\mathrm{KL}(q\,\|\,p)$ shrinks — but it cannot reach zero, because no product distribution can capture the tilt of a correlated Gaussian. The residual gap is the cost of the mean-field assumption.

Run CAVI on a target below and watch the ELBO rise while $\mathrm{KL}(q\,\|\,p)$ falls as the bound tightens.

params.title: Mean-field CAVI: ELBO up, KL down
params.hint: step coordinate ascent; ELBO + KL = log p(x) stays fixed
params.svgTitle: Coordinate-ascent variational inference tightening the evidence lower bound while the KL divergence to the posterior shrinks

6. MCMC & Gibbs sampling

Variational inference is fast but biased by its family. The complementary approach is to sample: draw configurations $x^{(1)},x^{(2)},\dots$ whose distribution converges to the target $p$, then estimate any expectation by a long-run average, $\mathbb{E}_p[h]\approx\frac1M\sum_t h(x^{(t)})$. We cannot sample $p$ directly — it has an intractable $Z$ — so we build a Markov chain whose stationary distribution is exactly $p$. This is Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC).

Gibbs sampling

The workhorse for graphical models is Gibbs sampling. Sweep the variables in turn, and resample each from its full conditional given the current values of all the others:

$x_i^{(t+1)}\ \sim\ p\big(x_i \mid x_{-i}^{(t)}\big)\ =\ p\big(x_i \mid x_{\mathcal{N}(i)}^{(t)}\big).$

The second equality is the §2 Markov-blanket property: the full conditional depends only on $x_i$'s neighbors, and the intractable global $Z$ cancels, so each draw is a cheap local computation. Each update leaves $p$ invariant; for a connected (ergodic) model the chain forgets its start and its marginal converges to $p$.

Why it works. Resampling $x_i$ from $p(x_i \mid x_{-i})$ preserves $p$ as the stationary distribution: if $x_{-i}$ is already distributed as $p$'s marginal, then redrawing $x_i$ from the exact conditional returns a sample from the full $p$. Composing such moves keeps $p$ invariant, and ergodicity then forces convergence — regardless of where the chain started. The samples are correlated across sweeps, not independent; that autocorrelation (the mixing time) is the price of MCMC.
Worked mini-example — Gibbs on two variables. For a correlated bivariate target, alternately draw $z_1\sim p(z_1 \mid z_2)$ then $z_2\sim p(z_2 \mid z_1)$. Each conditional of a Gaussian is itself Gaussian (a closed form), so each step is trivial; the chain traces a staircase that fills out the correlated cloud. The empirical histogram of the visited states converges to the true joint as the number of sweeps grows.

Run Gibbs sampling on the Ising grid below — each spin is resampled from its Markov-blanket conditional — and watch the empirical magnetization distribution settle toward the target as the chain mixes.

See also
  • Markov chains

Connections

Graphical models are the grammar that lets probability scale: the same factorization that compresses the joint also tells you, structurally, which inferences are linear-time and which are NP-hard, and the inference toolkit — elimination, message passing, variational bounds, MCMC — recurs across every quantitative science. Open frontiers are mostly about learning the structure and parameters from data, doing inference at the scale of deep models (amortized and stochastic variational inference, normalizing flows), and pushing causal versions of d-separation into reliable causal discovery. A beginner is often surprised that exact inference is hopeless in general (it is #P-hard) — the elegance of the factorization does not buy tractable answers for free.

  • Probability theory — conditional probability & Bayes' rule — every directed factor $p(x_i\mid\mathrm{pa}(i))$ and every posterior query is Bayes' rule applied locally on the graph.
  • Probability theory — Markov chains — MCMC is a Markov chain engineered to have the target as its stationary distribution; convergence rests on that theory.
  • Information theory — KL divergence — the ELBO is built from the KL between the variational $q$ and the true posterior, so variational inference is information geometry in disguise.
  • Statistical learning theory — empirical risk minimization — fitting a graphical model's parameters by maximum likelihood is regularized ERM, and the structure controls the model's capacity.
  • Random walks & mixing — MCMC and mixing times — how fast Gibbs sampling gives usable estimates is exactly a mixing-time question about the chain's spectral gap.

A Gaussian process is itself a graphical model — a jointly Gaussian field whose covariance kernel induces the (dense) dependency graph — so the kernel machinery and the graphical-model machinery describe the same object from two directions. Forward to come: deep generative models and probabilistic programming, where the graph is written as code and inference is automatic.
